Wall Street enters a correction: the Nasdaq falls 5.3% and wipes out its 2026 gains, Nvidia plunges 14%

On Friday, November 20, the S&P 500 lost 3.7% and the Nasdaq 5.3%, putting the latter back in the red for the year. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones are now more than 10% below their records: this is a “correction.” Nvidia fell 14%, and Anthropic gave back some of its first-day gains [1][2][3].

The S&P 500 closed at 6,910.39 points, down 265.44 points (−3.7%), according to the AP news agency [1]. It has lost more than 10% since its October 6 record: professionals call this a “correction” [2].

The Nasdaq, the tech-heavy index, plunged 5.3% to 22,617.73 points and is now down since January 1 [1][2]. The Dow Jones shed 949.73 points (−1.9%) to 48,147.33 points [4], the day after a 1,101-point drop.
Over the week, the S&P 500 lost 8.6%, the Dow Jones 8% and the Nasdaq 10%, according to StockTitan [4].

Nvidia, the world's leading maker of AI chips, ended at $125.53, down 14%, its seventh straight weekly decline, the longest streak since 2008 [5]. The stock is nearly 48% below its October 6 record [5].

Anthropic, which went public on Thursday at $83 a share, lost about 8.5% and ended at $88.30, just above its IPO price, according to CNN [3]. “There is a real exodus out of tech stocks,” sums up Steve Sosnick, a strategist at Interactive Brokers [3].

The shock went around the world: Tokyo's Nikkei lost 5.1%, Seoul's Kospi 5.2% and the Taiwan stock exchange 6.2%, its worst week since 1991 [7]. In Paris, the CAC 40 fell 1.89% to 7,927.75 points (−5.27% over the week) [8], and Germany's DAX 2.6% [9].

Key takeaway: Anthropic's record IPO was supposed to prove that AI was worth its prices. According to CNN, it has not changed what has been worrying Wall Street since October: possible new rules, AI investment that could slow down, overpriced stocks [10].

Nvidia is the focus of the doubts. Its CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang resigned on November 12; the board chair cited “personal conduct inconsistent with the code of conduct” [5]. Its enormous weight in the indexes drags down the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq.

A “correction” (−10% from the peak) is not yet a “bear market” (−20%). But the S&P 500 is only up 0.9% for the year, according to StockTitan [4]: the 2026 gains, driven by AI, have almost disappeared. And on Friday Donald Trump added uncertainty by threatening a “huge tax” on US companies that build data centers abroad [6].

The backdrop does not help: the Fed, the US central bank, is due to meet on December 8 and 9, and several of its officials are arguing for a rate hike [11]. Higher rates make risk-free investments more attractive than expensive stocks.
If you have unit-linked life insurance or a “world” fund, a large part of it is invested in the US tech giants, which fell sharply this week. As long as you don't sell, the loss remains on paper.

Trump threatens a “huge tax” on US giants that build data centers abroad, and targets a €13 billion Google project in Finland

On Friday, November 20, back from Asia, Donald Trump announced at a White House press conference that he would no longer let US companies build data centers outside the United States. He is threatening a “huge tax” and cited a Google project in Finland, without giving a rate or a timetable [1][2][4].

Speaking to the press, Donald Trump said his administration would not allow US companies to set up data centers abroad, under threat of a “huge tax” [1][3]. His argument: if these centers go to other countries, “China will take them all” [4].

He targeted a specific case: “They want to build one now in Finland, and we're not going to let that happen” [1]. This is Google's project worth about €13 billion (nearly $15 billion), announced in September, its biggest investment in Europe, in Hamina, Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala in 2027 and 2028 [1].

No rate, no legal mechanism and no date were announced, and it is unclear which projects would be targeted [1][10]. Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, which operate global networks of data centers, are the most exposed, according to NBC News [2].

The Finnish project had already been held back: the Finnish supervisory agency (LVV) had work suspended in Muhos and Kajaani after more than 300 hectares of forest were cleared without an impact assessment [1].

During the roughly 90-minute press conference, alongside JD Vance and Marco Rubio, he also said that Iran is “telling fibs” and that he could not “speak for America” when asked whether Vladimir Putin was a friend of the United States [5][7].

Facing the incoming Democratic Congress, he said he was ready to work with the opposition, while promising to veto unacceptable bills: “We could end up doing better than dealing only with Republicans” [5][6].
Key takeaway: after tariffs on goods, Donald Trump wants to apply “made in America” to artificial intelligence infrastructure, by threatening his own tech champions [1][2].
For countries that were counting on these investments, it is a heavy blow: Finland was expecting Google's biggest European project [1].

The paradox is political: the announcement comes less than three weeks after midterm elections lost by the Republicans, in which voters' concerns about data centers played a role. A majority of Americans say they are very worried about their effect on electricity prices and on water, according to a survey cited by NBC News [2].
Without a specific mechanism, the threat remains for now a bargaining chip, in a Washington where Republicans lose Congress in January [8][9].

The services you use every day (search engines, cloud storage, AI assistants) run in these data centers. If the US giants give up building them in Europe, your data is more likely to be stored in the United States, and Europe would lose jobs and AI investment.

India-Pakistan: a Pakistani minister in New Delhi for the first time since 2023, but India won't budge an inch on the Indus treaty

Musadik Malik, Pakistan's Minister of Climate Change, arrived in New Delhi on Friday, November 20, for a forum of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). It is the first visit by a Pakistani federal minister to India since May 2023. The same day, New Delhi repeated that there was “absolutely no change” on the Indus Waters Treaty [1][2][4].

Musadik Malik is leading the Pakistani delegation to the SCO's first “Dialogue of Civilizations,” from November 20 to 22 at Purana Qila, Delhi's Old Fort. He was welcomed by Pakistan's chargé d'affaires, is due to speak on Saturday morning and to meet other delegations on the sidelines of the forum [1].

The last Pakistani federal minister to visit India was Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, then foreign minister, for an SCO meeting in Goa in May 2023 [2]. Islamabad had first been invited to send its culture minister, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi. No bilateral meeting has been announced [2].

Asked about the future of relations, Musadik Malik replied: “All our relations will improve,” adding that “the tectonic plates of geopolitics are moving very fast” [3]. He avoided directly answering a question about cross-border terrorism, according to the Indian press [8].

The spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs, Randhir Jaiswal, said on Friday that India's position on the Indus Waters Treaty was “very clear” and that there was “absolutely no change” [4][5]. He stressed that the forum is multilateral and that all SCO members, Pakistan included, were invited [4].

He was asked the question because Musadik Malik is not in charge of culture and reportedly raised the Indus treaty [4]. India suspended this water-sharing treaty in 2025, after the April 22 Pahalgam attack, which killed 26 people [4].

Opening the forum, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi presented cultural ties as “the strongest guarantee of world peace” [6][7]. He proposed that SCO countries digitize and translate their ancient manuscripts, with the help of AI [6].
Key takeaway: this is a small opening in the freeze between two nuclear-armed neighbors, who fought for four days in May 2025, but New Delhi is keen that it not be seen as a thaw [2][4][9].

Water is at the heart of the conflict. In March 2026, India's ambassador to the UN, P. Harish, explained that the Indus treaty would remain suspended as long as Pakistan supported terrorism, and that Pakistan had refused to discuss changes [10]. Islamabad strongly denies supporting attacks in India [9].

The SCO framework lets the two countries cross paths without losing face: India invites all members, Pakistan sends a minister, and nobody talks about bilateral negotiations [2][4]. Narendra Modi wants this forum to become more than a ceremony, building on 25 years of SCO cooperation on security, the economy and transport [7].

India and Pakistan are two nuclear powers that went to war 18 months ago. Every sign of dialogue, however tentative, slightly reduces the risk of a new crisis that would shake the region and India, which has become a key trading partner for Europe. But for now, nothing is changing: no negotiations, no agreement on water.

news.2026-11-21-tunisie-sihem-ben-sedrin: Tunisia: Sihem Ben Sedrine, a figure of the fight against dictatorship, sentenced to five more years in prison, denounces a “political verdict”

On Friday, November 20, a Tunis court sentenced Sihem Ben Sedrine, former president of the Truth and Dignity Commission, which was tasked with judging the abuses of the former regime, to five years in prison without parole. Already sentenced to 25 years in June, the activist calls the decision “arbitrary”; Amnesty International denounces a “flagrant injustice” [1][4][5].
The sentence was handed down by the criminal chamber specializing in financial corruption of the Tunis court of first instance [1][2].

The case, known as the “Lazhar Sta” case after a businessman, concerns alleged irregularities in an arbitration-based reconciliation agreement concluded by the Truth and Dignity Commission (IVD) with this businessman [1][3].

Two other people were sentenced: Khaled Krichi, a former IVD member, to four years in prison, and former minister Mabrouk Korchid to six years, in absentia [1][2]. Khaled Krichi is in detention, while Sihem Ben Sedrine appeared in court as a free woman [1][4].
Sihem Ben Sedrine called the ruling a “political verdict” and an “arbitrary decision” taken by the political authorities [4][5].
This is not her first conviction: in June 2026, she had already received a total of 25 years in prison in several cases. She remains free pending the outcome of her appeals [4][5].
Amnesty International denounced a “flagrant injustice” targeting her work on transitional justice, that is, the examination of abuses committed under the former regime [5].

Key takeaway: in Tunisia, it is now those who investigated the abuses of the former regime who are being convicted. Sihem Ben Sedrine, a human rights activist, is the best-known symbol of this [4][5].

What she is accused of is not personal enrichment but the way the IVD concluded an arbitration-based reconciliation agreement with a businessman: the courts are judging this work of the commission before a chamber devoted to financial corruption, and are also convicting a former member and a former minister [1][2][3].

These trials come on top of a tense economic climate: in the third quarter of 2026, the Tunisian economy grew only 1.9% year on year, and unemployment affects about one young person in three [6][7]. The government highlights the fight against corruption, while its opponents see it as a way to silence critical voices [4][5].

Tunisia is a close neighbor of France, across the Mediterranean. These repeated convictions complicate Europe's relations with Tunis, with which it cooperates notably on migration. If you travel there, nothing changes day to day, but political debate is increasingly closed off.

Nvidia: seven weeks of decline, a first since 2008, and nearly half its value gone since October

On Friday, November 20, Nvidia fell 14% to $125.53 and posted its seventh straight weekly decline, the longest streak since the 2008 financial crisis. The stock has lost nearly 48% since its October 6 record. Jensen Huang's departure, the market regulator and Trump add to the doubts about AI [1][2].
The stock lost $20.45 on Friday (−14%), to $125.53, and is nearly 48% below its October 6 record, according to CNBC [1]. It is its ninth decline in ten sessions, according to the AP news agency [8].

According to Investing.com, it is Nvidia's worst week since October 2008 [2]. The stock was already down about 7% before a press report about an investigation by the SEC, the US market regulator, into its accounting practices deepened the fall [2].

The Wall Street Journal had reported as early as November 17 that the SEC had opened a civil investigation into whether Nvidia's communications had misled investors; the SEC says it does not comment on “the existence or nonexistence” of an investigation [4].

Jensen Huang, co-founder and head of the company since its creation, resigned on November 12; the new chair of the board cited the discovery of “personal conduct inconsistent with the code of conduct” [1].

On Friday, Donald Trump called Jensen Huang a “good man” who “made bad decisions,” and said he wanted “a big apology” and his return [5]. Huang said he was ready to come back, an offer Nvidia rejected [5].
The same day, the president threatened a “huge tax” on US companies that build data centers abroad, Nvidia's big customers [5].
Other chipmakers followed: Micron, Broadcom and AMD fell sharply [8].

Key takeaway: Nvidia has become the symbol stock of AI, and its fall is as much a matter of confidence as of numbers. In a few weeks, the company lost its founder, became the subject of an investigation reported by the press and saw the US president weigh in [1][4][5].

This is what financiers call “key-person risk”: when a company is closely associated with one leader, their sudden departure raises doubts about the strategy, customer relationships and governance [1].
Nvidia's weight in the indexes turns its troubles into a problem for the whole market: its fall on Friday weighed heavily in the Nasdaq's 5.3% decline [8].

Nvidia is in almost every fund that tracks the US or global market, including those in your life insurance or your PEA (French stock savings plan) through ETFs. Its drop of nearly half in six weeks shows that a single very large company can move all your savings.

How it works: “key-person risk” on the stock market

Some companies are so identified with their founder that investors buy the person as much as the company. Jensen Huang had led Nvidia since its creation. His sudden departure on November 12 [1] forces the market to ask who will set the strategy, who will negotiate with major customers and whether other problems will come out. An investigation by the market regulator [4] adds a risk of fines or restated accounts. As long as these uncertainties last, investors demand a lower price to hold the stock, which explains a steeper decline than in the rest of the sector.

news.2026-11-21-inde-bourse-refuge-ia.ti: During the AI crash, the Mumbai stock exchange climbs to a nine-month high: India becomes a safe haven for foreign investors
news.2026-11-21-inde-bourse-refuge-ia.su: On Friday, November 20, while Tokyo, Seoul and Taiwan plunged more than 5%, Mumbai's Sensex gained 1.08% and the Nifty 1.12%, reaching nine-month highs. Foreign funds, which are selling their AI stocks, have already invested a record amount in India this month [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-21-inde-bourse-refuge-ia.po: The Sensex closed at 83,919.71 points (+897.96 points, +1.08%) and the Nifty 50 at 25,800.60 points (+286.30 points, +1.12%), driven by banks and IT [3][7].

It is the fourth straight week of gains for the Indian stock market, bucking the trend in the rest of Asia, according to Reuters [2]. The MSCI Asia-Pacific stock index lost 8.5% over the week, its worst since 2020 [1].

According to Reuters, as of November 17 foreign investors had bought $9.53 billion of Indian stocks in November, a record for a single month [5]. The previous monthly record in rupees, from November 2020 (70,896 crore), has been far exceeded with 99,158 crore, according to Angel One [6].
More than half of these recent purchases went to banks and financial companies [2].
“The rotation of capital toward India was long overdue,” explains Sunny Agrawal of SBICAPS Securities, for whom the fall in AI stocks “highlights the bargains in India” [2].

Analysts also cite the drop in oil, most of which India imports, solid corporate earnings and favorable views from HSBC and Goldman Sachs [2]. One analyst notes that Brent has gone from about $118 to the low $90s [1].
Despite these record purchases, foreigners remain net sellers for 2026, to the tune of $21.88 billion as of November 17 [5].
news.2026-11-21-inde-bourse-refuge-ia.wh: Key takeaway: India is benefiting from the AI crash because it has few AI-related stocks. Its stock market is made up of banks, industrial groups and service companies, while Taiwan, Korea and Japan are full of chipmakers [2].

Large global funds spread their money across countries. When they sell Asian chip stocks, part of the money is reinvested in markets seen as shielded from the same risk: India benefits, after months of being neglected [2][5].

This strength remains fragile: it depends on continued foreign buying, moderate oil prices and a recovery in earnings, notes The Week [4]. If oil rises again, India's energy bill will weigh once more.
news.2026-11-21-inde-bourse-refuge-ia.fo: If you have an “emerging markets” fund or an India fund, this week shows the value of diversifying: the same crash does not hit every country the same way. But a market that rises thanks to foreign money can also fall quickly if that money leaves.

news.2026-11-21-inde-bourse-refuge-ia.de: How it works: capital “rotation” between countries

Large investment funds constantly compare countries and sectors. When a theme, here AI, becomes risky, they sell what is linked to it and look for markets that do not depend on it: this is “rotation.” Money leaving Taiwan or Seoul can thus end up in Mumbai, where banks and companies focused on domestic consumption dominate [2]. The massive inflow of dollars pushes up stocks, but also demand for rupees. The movement can reverse just as quickly when funds find better opportunities elsewhere.
news.2026-11-21-inde-bourse-refuge-ia.pa: Precedents: foreign money makes and breaks the Indian stock market
The Nifty hits its all-time high of 26,277.35 points and the Sensex 85,978.25 points, according to Business Standard [8].
Even at a nine-month high, the Nifty remains about 1.8% below this 2024 peak.
Foreigners pull out more than $8.5 billion in one month, a record [10], and the Nifty loses 6.2%, its worst month since March 2020 [9].
Foreign funds had then left for China, seen as cheaper: their flows can reverse abruptly.
Foreigners invest 70,896 crore rupees in Indian stocks in one month, the record broken this year [6].
Large waves of foreign buying have often accompanied strong rallies in the Indian stock market.
Indian indexes gain more than 8% in one week, their best week in over a year, with about 45,960 crore in net foreign purchases [11].
The rotation toward India began before the AI crash and accelerated with it.
news.2026-11-21-mexique-trump-accord-pro: Mexico: Trump says he is “close” to a trade deal, Sheinbaum accuses the opposition of seeking foreign interference ahead of 2027

Donald Trump said at the White House that the United States was “close” to a trade deal with Mexico, less so with Canada. On Friday, November 20, Claudia Sheinbaum defended the country's sovereignty and the 2027 elections [1][2][4].

“We're getting close to a deal,” Trump said, without a timetable. He said he had told Claudia Sheinbaum he believes the cartels run Mexico, and that the country had to correct its trade surplus with the United States [1][2].

Sheinbaum, who met Trump at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, hopes to seal the deal at the G20 in Miami in December, and cites progress on tariffs targeting cars, steel and aluminum [3]. Mexico City considers the 50% US tariffs on steel and aluminum unjustified [6].

At the parade marking the 116th anniversary of the Revolution, she told her opponents, whom she accuses of seeking foreign interference: “You will fail again in your attempt to delegitimize the 2027 elections” [4][5].
Key takeaway: the deal with Washington is getting closer, but Trump keeps linking trade and security, which leaves Mexico City little room to maneuver [1][2].

In July, Washington refused to extend the North American agreement (USMCA) for sixteen years [3]. Sheinbaum's sovereignty message is aimed as much at the opposition as at the United States, ahead of the 2027 midterm elections [4][5].
Many cars sold in Europe are assembled in Mexico: a deal that lowers US tariffs could change where these factories invest.

news.2026-11-21-thailande-arsenic-rivier: Thailand: arsenic at 30 times the standard in northern rivers polluted by Myanmar mines, Bangkok convenes a crisis unit

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul is convening government agencies this Saturday, November 21, to stop the arsenic poisoning the Kok, Sai and Ruak rivers in Chiang Rai province. The pollution is attributed to gold and rare earth mines in Shan State, Myanmar [1][4].

Arsenic readings reached 30 times the national standard for surface water in these three rivers [4]. Saturday's meeting, at 11 a.m. at Government House, is to study the location of small dams upstream to trap arsenic-laden sediment [4].
Anutin Charnvirakul called for urgent work with Myanmar [1]. A joint working group on water quality will meet in Bangkok on November 25 and 26, earlier than planned [1][3].
Four replacement drinking water projects are being prepared in three districts of Chiang Rai, for 345 households [3].
The Prime Minister raised the issue with Xi Jinping on the sidelines of APEC, and the Chinese president promised urgent assistance [2].
Key takeaway: the race for rare earths has an environmental cost that crosses borders, here from Myanmar to Thailand [1][4].
Thai officials and researchers link this pollution to unregulated rare earth mines in Myanmar [5]. Bangkok has therefore also asked Beijing for help [2][5].
Some of the rare earths in electric motors and wind turbines come from poorly controlled mines: their low price sometimes hides serious pollution.
